item.title: AI safety fears put OpenAI and Anthropic in the FTC's crosshairs
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.44
The Federal Trade Commission is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies over potential safety risks posed by their products, an agency spokesperson told Axios Wednesday. Why it matters: The federal government has largely taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI , but the FTC investigation could signal a shift for the industry. Driving the news: FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson is preparing civil investigative demands that would compel AI executives to turn over documents and testify about the safety of their models, according to the New York Post, which first reported the news. The probe has been underway for weeks, predating OpenAI's disclosure that models it was testing escaped their sandbox and compromised parts of AI platform Hugging Face's production infrastructure. OpenAI announced Monday that it would halt the release of its newest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after it performed poorly on safety testing. ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Between the lines: The recent push by top AI executives for increased guardrails around their technology has prompted some AI critics to question their motives. Ferguson recently said that AI firms are trying to panic Americans into pressuring policymakers to build a regulatory "moat" that would allow AI frontrunners to block smaller competitors from catching up. Catch up quick: News of the ongoing investigation comes just a day after top AI companies sent representatives to the White House to sign a pledge with President Trump to self-police their AI development. Trump compared it to something of a "constitution," but the rules the companies agreed to are similar to what they were already doing. Zoom out: The new reporting comes shortly after Axios exclusively reported that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers were investigating tens of thousands of potential security incidents, including some that had not previously been disclosed to the public. That reporting was later cited Monday when Florida's attorney general asked a court for a temporary injunction against OpenAI, alleging inadequate safety measures. On Tuesday, a public interest law group sued OpenAI over the Hugging Face breach, claiming, among other things, that the company was "knowingly employing an unfair business practice that threatens serious harm on the public." Go deeper... Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents Editor's note: Axios' Maria Curi contributed reporting.

item.title: Nvidia says new tool can contain rogue AI agents in "milliseconds"
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.14
Nvidia is deploying a new tool that it says can be used to prevent and contain rogue and potentially dangerous AI agents. Why it matters: The world's largest chip company has resisted calls to slow AI development over safety fears — arguing now that technological guardrails can keep rogue AI agents under control. Driving the news: Nvidia debuted the Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform, which includes its OpenShell open source software system and its Sentry agent monitoring system. The system "traces all actions" by agents running on Nvidia Vera CPUs, promising to "quarantine agents that attempt to move outside their boundaries in milliseconds." AI's "full promise can only be realized when people have confidence that AI is being built to be safe and deployed with wisdom and responsibility," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang wrote on X. "Safety is how trust is earned." State of play: OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which their frontier models took steps that outside evaluators would consider problematic, sources told Axios' Madison Mills last week. The episodes include bypassing guardrails, creating message boards, escaping sandboxes, website hijacking, self-prompting or seeking to bypass monitors. "Some of the agents even misreported what they did," Nvidia noted in a blog post Monday announcing its new platform. The intrigue: We're moving into a new era in which AI will be monitoring AI. And that will create more demand for chips — including the type that Nvidia sells — plus the data centers that use them and the power that's needed to run them. "If security agents or validation models are running alongside production agents, that creates another inference workload that did not previously exist," writes Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intel, at Circular Technology. Zoom out: The Nvidia tool rollout comes amid a feverish debate over whether rogue AI could destroy humanity. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon created a stir earlier this month when he resigned his post and warned on X that "the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt." The resulting conversation — which drew out more AI industry leaders making similar warnings — culminated in Huang himself dismissing the concerns as fearmongering.

item.title: Florida asks for order to halt ChatGPT development
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 1.14
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has asked for a temporary injunction against OpenAI and ChatGPT, claiming the company doesn't have the ability to properly regulate its own technology. Why it matters: The legal fight could further test how far states can go to restrict AI companies despite the federal government declining to enact guardrails. Florida's request specifically cites a Sept. 26 Axios scoop that OpenAI and Anthropic are facing tens of thousands of security incidents with their models, not the dozens that are publicly known. What they're saying: "Stop calling it safe," Uthmeier said in a video posted to X on Monday. "Stop pretending it's human. Stop selling it to kids. If Sam Altman meant what he said about slowing down, he can join our ask to the court. If he will not, we ask the court to do what OpenAI will not do for itself: protect Florida families." The other side: "People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do ourselves," OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said in a statement provided to Axios. The ChatGPT maker is "committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company," Pusateri added. Catch up quick: Uthmeier first sued OpenAI in June, alleging that the company violated Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act for being "negligent and grossly negligent in the design, marketing, sale, promotion, and distribution" of ChatGPT. The suit alleged that OpenAI "failed to warn Floridians of ChatGPT's dangers, fraudulently misrepresented the safety of ChatGPT, and created a public nuisance by releasing ChatGPT in Florida without proper safeguards." Zoom in: The motion details multiple instances in which OpenAI says its AI models bypassed safety restraints while completing tasks, including the Hugging Face hack. It also cites attempted hacks of U.S. government websites and an incident in which an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to an Australian health department site . The motion alleges OpenAI violates the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting personal information from children under 13 without parental consent and lacks adequate measures to prevent minors from accessing ChatGPT. It adds that "[i]n examining the way ChatGPT interacts with minors, researchers have 'wanted to test the guardrails [of ChatGPT]. The visceral initial response is, 'Oh my Lord, there are no guardrails.'" Zoom out: The motion cites reporting from Axios' Madison Mills that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving problematic model behavior, including "bypassing guardrails, creating message boards, escaping sandboxes, website hijacking, self-prompting or seeking to bypass monitors." The incidents vary in severity, and most investigated so far are not known to have caused real-world harm. OpenAI recently announced it was pausing training on its most capable models and would resume only when additional safeguards and "alignment improvements" are in place. Go deeper: AI pioneers warn of an "intelligence explosion" Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout. It has been corrected to reflect that Florida requested a temporary injunction (not an emergency injunction).

item.title: Scoop: Rubio ordered Iranian delegation to leave the country, U.S. official says
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanded on Monday that the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly immediately leave the country after negotiations stalled, according to a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters: Though the Iranians were likely to depart soon anyway, Rubio's move was a highly unusual diplomatic rebuke and laid bare the deep distrust between the two countries amid fruitless efforts to broker an end to the war. Qatari mediators tried to secure a diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran but made little progress, with neither side willing to budge. Among those ordered to leave New York was Rubio's Iranian counterpart, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. What they're saying: "Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome. The UN General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go," the U.S. official said. Behind the scenes: On Monday morning, the White House thought there might be progress in talks with Iran later in the day. But by late afternoon it became clear negotiations were at a stalemate. Then on Monday evening, at Rubio's orders, the U.S. mission to the UN told the Iranian mission to the UN that Araghchi's delegation had to leave New York immediately, according to the U.S. official. The Iranian delegation, including Araghchi, left for the airport several hours later and boarded a flight from New York to Doha at 1:20 a.m. Tuesday. A second source confirmed that the U.S. demanded that the Iranian delegation leave, but said Araghchi was scheduled to travel back to Tehran on Monday night anyway. What's next: Qatari mediators are continuing to talk to both sides about their compromise proposal, regional sources say. "Maybe I will blow 'em up," President Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked how he can reach a deal with a regime he says is crazy. "Maybe I blow 'em up. We have to make that decision. We will blow 'em up or make a deal. But the time is coming. It's gonna end very soon one way or the other."

item.title: Fed watchdog clears former chair Powell in renovation probe
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A Federal Reserve watchdog found no criminal wrongdoing by former chair Jerome Powell in its investigation of the central bank's expensive headquarters renovation, according to a report released on Wednesday. Why it matters: The findings effectively clear Powell after the Justice Department opened an unprecedented criminal investigation into then-Fed chair, which became public in January. What they're saying: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the Office of Inspector General wrote in the report. The watchdog added that it "did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation." Yes, but: While the report clears Powell, it faults Fed management and oversight of the project as construction costs more than doubled to $2.5 billion . The Fed "did not take numerous actions available to it that could have better controlled costs and mitigated some of the significant construction cost increases," the report says. Flashback : The renovation became a flashpoint in President Trump's broader campaign against Powell and the Fed. Trump toured the construction site with Powell in July 2025 and publicly challenged him over the project's soaring costs. Zoom out: The Justice Department's investigation centered on Powell's June 2025 testimony to Congress about the renovation and its rising costs. Powell denied wrongdoing and argued at the time that the investigation was part of a broader effort to pressure the Fed over interest rates. DOJ closed the investigation in April as the Fed's inspector general continued its review. Zoom in: The watchdog said that inflation alone could not explain the project's higher costs. For instance, the report shows that two major mechanical, electrical and plumbing contracts more than tripled to $539 million from an earlier $178 million estimate, far outpacing the broader rise in construction costs. Of note : The report says that the key design features that drew scrutiny from Congress and other critics — including marble, water features and a garden terrace — did not materially contribute to the project's cost increases. The Fed removed four planned new fountains in June 2025 because officials worried about "external stakeholders, such as Congress and the media, raising concerns about the design," according to the report. What to watch: Powell has remained on the Fed's board after his term as chair ended in May — an unusual move that he said was tied to seeing the investigation through to its conclusion. item.title: Exclusive: HHS launches project to speed up clinical trials
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The Trump administration on Wednesday is launching an effort to reimagine the way clinical trials are designed, with a goal of drastically reducing the time and money it takes to develop new drugs. Why it matters: The program, shared first with Axios, could provide a template for reconfiguring the drug development process and boosting U.S. competitiveness in the global biotech race. Driving the news: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health Director Alicia Jackson are unveiling the new effort in Austin, Texas. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and FDA Acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas will also attend the announcement. The effort — dubbed the Simulation-augmented, Real-time Platform Adaptive Seamless Trials (SURPASS) program — features teams selected through a bidding process that will bring drug candidates through experimental clinical trial processes. How it works: The initiative under ARPA-H will begin by soliciting ideas from "teams" that include a drug sponsor. Winners will receive funding and support over five years. ARPA-H is looking for proposals that innovate in three technical areas: Phaseless trials that allow faster trials with fewer patients, the ability to analyze data in real time during the trial instead of than only when it ends, and using automation to reduce inefficiencies. Teams will also likely include medical centers or other clinical sites, biostatisticians, and companies that have the ability to predict drug outcomes via a computer. The FDA has been included in the planning of the program, and "there won't be any surprises for regulators in this," said Daria Fedyukina, the program manager. The big picture: One of the reasons China has become such a popular location for drug manufacturers is because it's much cheaper and faster to do early-stage clinical trials there. Experts and the biopharmaceutical community largely agree that in order to compete, the U.S. needs to streamline its trial processes. Today, developing a drug can take longer than a decade and cost around $2 billion. More than 90% of drug candidates fail, according to HHS. What they're saying: "The goal is to develop the tech that is missing and blaze the trail of a new clinical trial paradigm," Fedyukina said. The program will require the development of "blueprints and standards that then can be deployed and used by all other trials in the U.S," she added. While "it's hard to put a number to how much cost savings or time savings we can achieve," Fedyukina said, "there is no reason why we cannot target, let's say, a 10x reduction in the cost of clinical development for a drug." "There's no reason why we cannot cut timeline in half or more," she added. Details: ARPA-H is also announcing three related projects today aimed at improving the infrastructure around clinical trials. One is focused on setting up more clinical trial sites, with the help of AI to speed up site activation and prepare sites that haven't held trials before. This will allow patients who live near hospitals that don't currently participate in clinical trials to gain access to experimental drugs they may benefit from. The other two projects focus on clinical trial data infrastructure and helping patients with complex cancers benefit from their own data and better navigate the care system. The bottom line: This is all an experiment, but if successful it could pay big dividends.

item.title: "Strong indications" Iran had role in U.K. bomb plot, PM Andy Burnham says
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are "strong indications that Iran played a part" in a suspected bomb plot at a British air base used by the U.S. The big picture: Burnham's comments to the BBC come after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the weekend incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands ‌of a foreign actor." Tehran denies any involvement. Five British men were released on bail Monday following their arrest a day earlier in connection with the alleged plot. What they're saying: "We will say more in due course but we can confirm ... that we believe Iran to have played a part," Burnham told the BBC, declining to elaborate. He emphasized that the counter-terrorism investigation is ongoing and "complex" and that investigators are "working closely with our colleagues" in the U.S. Rubio told Fox News Monday that the incident "ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world — and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally." Context: U.K. earlier this year allowed the U.S. Air Force to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps named RAF Fairford in July when it said that any British base used for attacks on Iranian territory would be considered a "legitimate target."

item.title: Kash Patel's FBI loses another top official
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Andrew Bailey, deputy director of the FBI, is leaving his post after just over a year of service, Bailey and Director Kash Patel confirmed Monday. Why it matters: Bailey's resignation adds to turnover under Patel, as top aides and experienced security officials have left the agency. What they're saying: "With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri," Bailey wrote on X Monday. "I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence." Replying to Bailey's post, Patel said he was thankful for his service and that his "fantastic contribution[s] instituting critical reforms which resulted in our historic success will live on. Andrew's leadership at the FBI will be missed but we are grateful he answered the call to serve!" When initially reached for comment, the FBI directed Axios to Bailey's Monday morning X post. Zoom in: Bailey, Missouri's former attorney general, oversaw some of the FBI's election security efforts, making his departure a little more than a month before the midterms particularly notable. Bailey was also in charge of the FBI's raid on the Fulton County Election Hub and Operation Center in Georgia in January, where agents seized ballots and other documents related to the 2020 election, according to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi . Yes, but: A senior administration official familiar with Bailey's departure told Axios' Marc Caputo that Bailey didn't have much of a portfolio on election security or otherwise. "The short answer is no: Bailey wasn't doing anything," the official said. "He did nothing on voter fraud, nothing on election integrity. He quit because he had nothing to do." The other side: When Axios contacted the FBI for comment on the official's remarks, a spokesperson rejected the criticism. "This is false," the spokesperson said. "Co-Deputy Director Bailey's portfolio included election integrity, on which the FBI has been doing a lot, as well as partner engagement – again, where FBI has had a heavy presence." Catch up quick: Bailey was first tapped to serve as co-deputy director alongside Dan Bongino last August, an uncommon dual-leadership arrangement. Many FBI agents believed Bondi brought Bailey in as a potential successor if President Trump soured on Patel, the New York Times reports . Bondi left her post as attorney general in April. Bongino announced last December that he was leaving the FBI to return to podcasting. After Bongino departed, Christopher Raia, the former head of the FBI's New York field office, was tapped to serve as co-deputy director alongside Bailey. Go deeper: Patel defends FBI hiring changes involving bestiality, prostitution Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout. Marc Caputo contributed reporting.

item.title: SpaceX brings Starship home early after first orbital flight
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
SpaceX's next-generation Starship rocket came back to Earth earlier than planned after its first orbital flight Monday, with an explosion visible on the company's livestream just after touchdown in the Pacific Ocean. Why it matters: The massive, fully-reusable Starship is key to SpaceX's commercial spaceflight ambitions, while NASA is counting on a modified version for use as a lunar lander in its Artemis program. Driving the news: Starship launched from South Texas just before 9 a.m. ET on a planned test flight of about 10 hours. It was set to orbit Earth about six times before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean, west of Chile. But SpaceX decided to bring it back to Earth after only about 3 hours. As part of the mission, Starship deployed 26 of the company's new, better-performing Starlink V3 internet satellites. The cause of the apparent explosion was not immediately clear, and the company didn't offer any details. Zoom in: Starship's first-stage Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf of America shortly after launch. SpaceX says this Super Heavy was modified after ice clogging issues interfered with a splashdown attempt on the last test flight. What they're saying: " Flight tests until this point have intentionally flown passively safe suborbital trajectories to maximize public safety while allowing for maximum learning," SpaceX says in a mission summary. "By going to orbit, the next phase of developing Starship to be fully and rapidly reusable can begin." What's next: SpaceX plans to eventually "catch" Starship in the arms of its launch tower — a feat it's accomplished with Super Heavy, but not Starship — but didn't make the attempt this time. Editor's note: This story has been updated with the latest developments.

item.title: "Window for action may close" if AI begins improving itself, AI pioneers warn
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Some of the world's foremost AI researchers and policy leaders — including at OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft — are warning that AI's growing ability to automate its own development could rapidly speed up its progress. Why it matters : Such a rapid scale-up in capabilities would leave governments and institutions with little time to prepare for or respond to the consequences, they say. In one scenario, they caution, a year's worth of advances could occur in a matter of weeks. The warning's authors include Turing Award winners such as Geoffrey Hinton, as well as OpenAI's chief scientist, Microsoft's chief scientific officer and a co-founder of Anthropic. Driving the news : In a new white paper, they say AI models that can automate the process of improving themselves will create an "intelligence explosion." The paper points to evidence that AI systems at Anthropic and OpenAI are beginning to perform more internal research and development tasks and automate a sizable proportion of engineering tasks. How it works : Those developments indicate that the two companies are edging closer to the threshold of "recursive self improvement, " whereby AI systems improve themselves rapidly. The authors estimate that once AI models reach expert-level R&D capabilities, it will be possible for a developer to support an AI workforce equal to millions of top human researchers. Catch up quick : The warning comes after Axios revealed that OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which frontier models took steps that outside evaluators would consider problematic. The incidents, which for the most part aren't known to have caused real-world harm, raise questions about how much the companies — or any top AI developer — can control their technology. As capabilities expand further, the researchers warn that society is unprepared. Reality check : The authors say such an intelligence explosion is far from certain. A number of developments could prevent many of the RSI scenarios they present, including computing constraints, automation challenges, diminishing returns from expanding capabilities or time-consuming training runs. Zoom in : Hinton's participation is noteworthy, as he is widely credited with laying the intellectual foundations for today's boom, although he has warned about what he expected would be negative side effects of AI for years. Since leaving Google, Hinton has been among the loudest voices about AI's potential dangers and has discussed the risks from widespread job displacement, cyberattacks, biological weapons and other concerns. The researchers call for greater government visibility into AI R&D automation, ways to pause or slow its acceleration if needed, and more preparation for its impact. They suggest mandatory reporting of incidents, independent evaluators, safety requirements for testing powerful systems and creating ways to pause certain AI work. The bottom line : The paper's authors acknowledge the uncertainty about RSI and its impact but say that if it does occur, there will be little time to make adjustments. "Once an intelligence explosion begins," the paper says, "the window for action may close."

item.title: Exclusive: AI giants, unions join forces for data center fight
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
AI companies, private equity firms and unions are looking beyond 2026 in the data center debate , banding together to form a new multimillion-dollar coalition to make the case for responsible growth in seven key states. Why it matters: The new group, the American Infrastructure Alliance, wants to partner with state and local officials to create standards and guardrails for data centers in 2027. In return, the coalition hopes to head off moratoriums on new construction. The group is planning initial campaigns in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, Pennsylvania, Indiana and South Carolina. The alliance is backed by Blackstone, OpenAI, QTS and SoftBank Group, along with key unions, including the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW). What they're saying: "Responsible growth requires clear expectations for everyone involved," said Tag Greason, co-CEO of QTS, the Blackstone-owned data center operator. "Blanket bans on necessary infrastructure projects would set back our economy and threaten good middle-class jobs," said Kenneth Cooper, the IBEW's international president. "The IBEW is committed to responsible development that benefits workers, communities and our nation." "We are proud to join this coalition to chart a clear path forward, so that UA members can continue to protect the health of the nation," said Mark McManus, general president of the United Association of Union Plumbers and Pipefitters (UA) . Between the lines: This isn't an outside group built to flood the airwaves in key congressional races or battleground states ahead of the 2026 midterms. Instead, it represents an initial investment in a broader battle over AI and data centers that will likely bleed into the 2027 state legislative battles and the 2028 presidential campaign. "Texas shouldn't choose between protecting what matters and building what's next," the narrator says in one of its ads , which makes an appeal to Gov. Greg Abbott (R). "We can do both." Zoom out: Data centers have become a defining issue in the 2026 midterm elections, with Democrats hammering Republicans in key states for supporting them. Leading progressives, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), have unveiled legislation to pause all new data center construction nationwide until AI safeguards are in place. At the state level, Abbott — a cheerleader for data centers before the political backlash to them began — halted approvals for new data centers in early August. A few weeks later, he said data center companies had "dug their own grave" and deserved the backlash they were facing. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) had a similar reversal: Last year he celebrated a $20 billion Amazon investment, but last month signed an executive order to tighten the rules for data center development. Zoom in: Unions are heavily represented in the group, with the goal of activating their members to help convince state and local officials that data centers can be built responsibly. Besides the IBEW, the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers (SMART), the International Association of Heat and Frost Insulators and Allied Workers (HFIAW), the International Association of Iron Workers, and the United Association of Union Plumbers and Pipefitters (UA) are aboard. The group's own polling found that data centers are deeply unpopular in Ohio, with 67% of those surveyed holding an unfavorable opinion, compared with 18% who have a favorable impression. But those numbers flip when data centers pledge to keep electricity costs low, create jobs and generate tax revenue, according to the group's polling. The bottom line: The group wants to work with local officials — not against them. "American workers and communities should have a seat at the table as this critical infrastructure is built," said Michael Coleman, general president of SMART.

item.title: AI's man of the moment
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Dario Amodei went from a MAGA smear campaign target, to a "Saturday Night Live" punching bag, to a private White House dinner with President Trump — all in the space of 72 hours this weekend. Such is life for the face of AI in America. The big picture: He may not have sought the status, but Anthropic's quirky, intellectual CEO has become the frontman for a technology that seems to be changing the world by the day. In the history of capitalism, there has seldom been a more unusual spokesman for a transformative industry. A physicist by training with links to effective altruism , Amodei runs Anthropic in a way some inside and outside the company have compared to a religious leader . His penchant for being plain-spoken — especially when it comes to the risk of disaster — has earned him admirers and critics in equal measure, although he has remained consistent in his positions for years. The SNL sketch captured what often frustrates allies about him: calling for more regulation and a slowdown to establish greater safety, while accelerating the theory that he and Anthropic are best-equipped to be at the vanguard. A looming IPO could make him one of the world's multibillionaires, provided he doesn't scare everyone off first. The intrigue: OpenAI's Sam Altman does more press, and fits the traditional CEO mold much more neatly. But despite that — or, perhaps, precisely because he's more unvarnished — Amodei has become the first thing people think of when they think of AI. Between the lines: Consider how Anthropic spent the last few days. ⚠️ On Thursday, Axios's Maria Curi and Marc Caputo scooped a new MAGA memo doing the rounds at the White House that sought to paint Amodei as the poster child of the effective altruism movement, a recent bogeyman for conservatives who want a more muscular future for AI. (Anthropic has said Amodei doesn't identify as an effective altruist but is sympathetic to some of its tenets.) 🍽️ By Sunday, Maria and Marc scooped that President Trump had personally invited Amodei to dinner. (A dinner critics tried to head off by trashing him directly to the president hours beforehand.) In between, Amodei got the SNL treatment — an unflattering "Weekend Update" skit that painted him as barely able to complete a sentence without saying AI was going to kill us all. Stunning stat: Anthropic didn't even exist six years ago. In less than a decade, Amodei will have gone from a somewhat obscure scientist to one of the most important people in human history. item.title: Why I'm finally giving Meta AI a chance
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Meta is finally promising the one feature that has long kept me away from its AI services: privacy . Why it matters: In a world with many models capable of meeting my needs, knowing how my data will be used is a key factor, especially with sensitive information. Driving the news: The Facebook parent, which once called dibs on nearly any data one shared with Meta AI, has in recent months begun to sing a new tune. In a 6,500-word August manifesto , CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a broad promise. "People should have a fully private mode for personal agents where even Meta or any other service provider cannot see or grant access to your information." With the debut of Muse, Meta said users can choose which apps the viral assistant connects to and opt out of having interactions train its models. Muse data also won't feed Meta's ad systems, and a more ambitious confidential virtual machine option, encrypted with a key held only by the user, is still to come. Last week, Meta said it plans to bring private processing to AI glasses by year-end, protecting data even while it's processed in the cloud, though it hasn't committed to a date. Zoom in: I decided to give Meta a chance. I've started (tentatively) using Muse. I turned the setting off that allows Meta to train its systems on my data and am also eagerly awaiting the confidential option. For now, I'm using Muse to handle the sorts of things that I don't care if Facebook knows about me, or more accurately, things Facebook already knows. I asked my Muse agent on Thursday to alert me as soon as the time was set for the Golden State Valkyries' first playoff game. I woke up on Friday to a note from Muse letting me know the schedule had been announced. I also asked it to recommend an option for an easily removed, portable CarPlay display that I could use in a car I park on the street, and it gave me a number of reasonable recommendations. I've been a big user of Meta glasses since the first version — one that didn't even have AI capabilities to speak of. What sold me was the ability to use the cameras to record sports, pets and kids — interactions that are better suited to being able to stay in the moment rather than pulling out a phone. Over time, the glasses have gained AI features , but knowing that any photo or other data I uploaded to its servers could be used for ad targeting and other purposes was a nonstarter. I've given Meta a hard time about this, frequently pressing CTO Andrew Bosworth. Yes, but: This is a very tentative endorsement based on what Meta says it is going to do — and its track record on privacy is more than checkered. (See Friday's verdict from a New Mexico jury.) Zuckerberg says Meta will take a cut of transactions made with Muse and that will allow it to offer the service free for most customers. But he also once promised to bring end-to-end encryption to all of Meta's messaging surfaces, before retreating on some commitments. And there are other privacy concerns that remain unaddressed by Meta's latest announcements, especially when it comes to the rights of bystanders whose likenesses are being captured by the Ray-Bans I and others wear. "Meta's products that embed microphones and cameras in everyday devices pose serious privacy risks," Electronic Privacy Information Center executive director Alan Butler told Axios. The bottom line: Trust, but verify. I'm willing to dabble with using Muse and Meta AI on my glasses. But I'm not ready to hand over the keys to the castle.

item.description:

The U.S. military in recent weeks sent two additional Patriot missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, two U.S. officials and one regional source said. Why it matters: The U.S. wanted to reassure both allies that it would protect their key energy facilities in case President Trump decides to resume major combat operations against Iran. Trump said on Thursday that he's considering renewing a bombing campaign in the coming weeks. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said. Flashback: In early August, when Trump was considering launching a massive attack that included strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure, the leaders of both Saudi Arabia and Qatar lobbied him not to do it. They expressed grave concern that Iran would strike their oil and natural gas facilities in retaliation. U.S. officials said the pleas were a key reason Trump decided not to attack and move instead toward an economic pressure campaign. Behind the scenes: Last month, the U.S. military sent one additional Patriot battery to Saudi Arabia to protect a key oil facility. Another Patriot battery was sent to Qatar to protect a natural gas facility. The U.S. will need Saudi Arabia to allow it to use the country's airspace if major combat operations resume. But the Saudis are unlikely to grant permission if they feel oil facilities won't be protected. A spokesman for U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Capt. Tim Hawkins, declined to comment. Reality check: Patriot batteries and especially their interceptors have become a highly sought-after commodity since the war in Iran started. The U.S. military transferred batteries and interceptors to the Middle East from other regional commands, raising concerns about readiness in other parts of the world. State of play: The U.S. military is sending more warships, fighter jets and troops to the Middle East ahead of a possible resumption of the war. A U.S. official said the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its strike group left San Diego "quietly" on Sunday heading to the region. It's expected to arrive in the Middle East around mid-November. The Roosevelt will join the USS George H.W. Bush, which has been in the region since March, and the USS George Washington, which was sent from Japan during the summer and has been in the region for only about a month. "This means the Middle East region could potentially have up to three aircraft carrier strike groups. This is much more firepower," the U.S. official said. "Affordability and borrower demand have weakened in recent weeks as the higher-rate environment continues to put pressure on both prospective homebuyers and homeowners looking to refinance," MBA CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement. What we're watching: There are early signs that rising rates could put downward pressure on prices as sellers look to attract buyers. Reality check: Rates may not remain elevated for long. "We expect the situation to improve next year, as energy prices drop back and the aggressive Fed tightening cycle which has been priced into money markets does not fully materialise, causing mortgage rates to retrace most of their recent increases," Capital Economics senior North America economist Thomas Ryan wrote Tuesday. item.title: Lawyers: Pike getting "life-saving care" after failed execution
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike's attorneys said she was "in critical condition" and "receiving life-saving care" Thursday, a day after she survived an execution attempt during which the state administered two doses of the lethal injection drug. A death penalty expert told the Associated Press that Pike's survival after receiving the execution drug was unprecedented. The latest: State and federal elected officials are pressing for public accountability after the second failed execution this year. Gov. Bill Lee halted further executions for the rest of the year and ordered a independent review of the Pike execution attempt. On Thursday morning, he told reporters there were "very few answers" about what had gone wrong. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the frontrunner to succeed Lee as governor next year, blasted the "botched process" in a statement and pushed for the state to "bring back the electric chair." Pike's attorneys told reporters Thursday that Lee's pledge to launch an investigation did not go far enough. They urged him to commute her death sentence. What they're saying: Attorney Randy Spivey, who was inside the prison during the execution attempt, said prison officials spent about an hour trying to establish IV access. He counted at least seven needles used in Pike's left arm alone. Pike complained of sharp pain during the lethal injection. Spivey said he noticed her right arm turning purple, especially after the second round of chemicals. He said the lawyers had also been told of blistering and burning around the injection sites. Between the lines: Federal public defender Stephen Ferrell said the lawyers had warned courts months earlier about medical problems with Pike's veins that made it harder to establish an IV. Zoom in: The attorneys also said they weren't able to quickly reach their colleagues or court officials responsible for overseeing the execution. Spivey said it took seven minutes and passage through six locked doors to get to a telephone so he could reach the rest of Pike's legal team. Ferrell said an emergency telephone number provided for the Tennessee Supreme Court went to voicemail. The state's response: Lee called the latest failed execution "a tragedy" on Thursday morning. "It's deeply disturbing to me that that has happened in this state," he told reporters, according to Reuters. The big picture: This isn't the first time Tennessee's prison officials have faced scrutiny for their approach to the death penalty. After a 2022 execution was halted over failures to properly test the drugs , Lee paused all executions so the state could investigate and overhaul its lethal injection protocol. Executions resumed last year. But more problems surfaced in 2026. Tennessee prison officials abruptly stopped another inmate's execution in May after staff had difficulties finding a vein for an IV line used in the lethal injection. Critics blasted prison officials for disregarding Pike's concerns that there might be similar problems during her execution. Zoom out: Pike was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 beating death of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Her legal team does not contest her guilt. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, traveled to Nashville this week to witness the execution. "It was a mess," she told NBC News early Thursday. "They went to try to execute her, and she didn't die." Martinez vented her anger with the governor and prison officials: "They f----- up."

item.title: The Fed's long-term interest rate problem
item.description:

The relentless rise in long-term interest rates is starting to have effects on more parts of the economy, Kansas City Fed president Jeff Schmid told Axios Thursday. Collins said AI investment is also helping drive the solid economic growth that has persisted despite higher borrowing costs. "I think it does have broader effects, not just in particular sectors," Collins said. But it "remains to be seen" whether investment will continue at its current pace, she added. The intrigue: Schmid likened the Fed's challenge of separating strong demand from supply-driven inflation to a seven-layer dip — one of his favorite foods. "The beauty of a seven-layer dip is you have equal amounts of beans and sour cream," Schmid said. Right now, with AI and data centers, "there's too much beans in that dip," he added. "And not enough chips!" quipped Barkin.

item.title: The world opinion shifts on trade
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
More countries are buying into a core piece of President Trump's argument about what is broken in global trade, even as his tariffs rattle the world economy. Why it matters: Two major agreements over the past month show that more countries are embracing the view that huge trade imbalances and excess production can hurt domestic industries and may warrant action. Driving the news: G20 trade officials are in Milwaukee this week, where they announced a new agreement to tackle the global steel glut. The "Milwaukee Framework" calls on countries to curb market-distorting subsidies and step up monitoring of steel imports and trade circumvention. It also endorses "evidence-based actions" against excess capacity, including possibly tariffs. That agreement follows a broader acknowledgment at the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, N.C., in September. The U.S. and nearly every other G20 economy there agreed that large, persistent trade imbalances can harm other countries. They signed on to a statement that asked nations with big surpluses to address policies that leave them overly reliant on exports for growth. China was the lone G20 member present to object to that statement. Between the lines: For decades, governments have warned about distortions in global trade, including excess steel production. What is changing: the willingness to acknowledge the damage to domestic industries and protect them. "Most countries agree with these global issues, people agree with the diagnosis, but they're loath to action," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters on the sidelines of the conference. He said the Milwaukee agreement "couldn't have happened in 2015." "All these other countries — they know that if they want to continue to have access to the U.S. market, we need to adjust the international system," Greer said. "As we come with creative ideas and new structures and cohesive plans, they're coming on board." Zoom out: EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič welcomed the administration's focus on excess capacity at a roundtable with Greer and manufacturing CEOs at Rockwell Automation's Milwaukee headquarters on Tuesday. European industries are being crushed by cheap imports driven by global overcapacity, much of it from China. Europe is responding with more trade barriers of its own — possibly including harsher tariffs. "I think a lot of folks in Europe, including the trade commissioner and others, I think they're pretty clear-eyed about this issue…. They're starting to go through some of the steps we started going through 10 years ago," Greer said, adding he believes Europe itself contribute to global excess capacity. The other side: U.S. trading partners are dealing with tariffs, or the prospect of tariffs, aimed at some of the same problems they are working with Washington to address. Most Canadian steel exports to the U.S. face a 50% tariff. An import ban on certain Canadian products took effect as one of the nation's trade officials arrived in Milwaukee. Greer is also investigating excess capacity and production in 16 economies — probes that could ultimately clear the way for fresh tariffs. Greer acknowledged that tension at the roundtable, noting that the U.S. and its trading partners may have disputes with one another but still share concerns about excess production elsewhere. The intrigue: Foreign trade ministers piled into coach buses yesterday afternoon for a 1.5-mile trip to Rockwell Automation's Milwaukee headquarters, where they toured the factory floor. The "field trip" was intended to show the kind of advanced domestic manufacturing the Trump administration wants to encourage. Rockwell gave the ministers steel-toed sneakers for the tour (which were made in Vietnam). Zoom in: Rockwell, which makes automation technology used on factory floors, is investing $2 billion in U.S. plants, talent and technology. But tariffs are also raising costs for the manufacturer. Rockwell told investors over the summer that some of its customers are delaying projects. "In such a volatile environment with respect to tariffs and inflation, they want to make sure that the cost side of their business case is solid," CEO Blake Moret said on the company's earnings call. The bottom line: Trump-era tariffs are divisive, but the president's case for rethinking the global trading system is proving less so.

item.title: The rocky road to a new permitting law
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
A sweeping bipartisan deal to cut permitting red tape faces a long road ahead despite a broad show of support. Why it matters: Cutting hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors, but some green groups fear erosion of safeguards. Powerful business groups want to make building all sorts of infrastructure easier. Driving the news: Top Republicans and Democrats on the Senate's energy and environment panels on Wednesday dropped the 417-page bill that includes: New limits on the duration of lawsuits, and the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act. A stronger federal hand in siting and approval of large transmission projects. Protections for previously issued permits, a priority for renewables groups and Dems upset with Trump administration barriers. The big picture: A who's who of major business and energy industry groups — representing oil and gas , renewables and coal — cheered the bill. The White House backs the deal and wants quick passage, an official said. State of play: The deal still has a long road ahead. Co-author Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said Wednesday at a press conference that there will be revisions as backers seek input from colleagues. There are also "unresolved" questions about Trump officials returning to "regular order" for wind and solar projects, Whitehouse said. But he credited the administration with a "very reasonable opening proposal" on the matter. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee, criticized the bill and said his party will have a stronger hand next year. Center-left backers see a huge opening to help build out clean energy and grid upgrades to integrate it. But groups on the left flank of the climate movement panned it , calling it a giveaway to fossil fuel interests. What we're watching: Some groups with close ties to Democrats staked out a noncommittal-to-positive position, saying they need more time to study the bill. The Natural Resources Defense Council cheered transmission pieces while saying it's unclear if they outweigh "rollbacks" of environmental laws, and said it "must improve." Evergreen Action welcomed project certainty and transmission sections but added that changes to key environmental laws demand "diligent scrutiny." Zoom in: The bill would prevent utility ratepayers from bearing the costs of new power and grid upgrades needed for AI data centers. Everyone's still digesting the intricate bill, but in principle, turning this bipartisan goal into firm requirements could ease political hurdles. The bottom line: Two things are true — the odds of a big permitting deal are at their highest in a very long time, and many things could trip this up. item.title: Jack Smith faces new lawsuit over congressional phone records
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.34
Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sued former special counsel Jack Smith Wednesday, alleging he unlawfully obtained her cellphone toll records during his investigation of Trump and the 2020 election Why it matters: The lawsuit escalates Republicans' efforts to challenge Smith's investigation more than a year after his probe ended. What they're saying: "Through his Arctic Frost witch hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the President of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation's history," Blackburn said. "This lawsuit is solely about holding Mr. Smith accountable and ensuring that our nation's justice system can never again be weaponized against the American people. I thank the New Civil Liberties Alliance for their partnership in filing this complaint and for fighting to uphold our cherished constitutional rights." Driving the news: The suit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee one day after Smith testified at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing Tuesday. The suit alleges Smith obtained a nondisclosure order without telling the judge that the underlying subpoena sought the records of a sitting senator. Blackburn's cellphone provider was ordered to keep the subpoena secret. Blackburn is asking the court to award her $1 in nominal damages to emphasize that she isn't seeking money but instead wants to hold Smith accountable for his allegedly unlawful actions. Legal counsel for Smith did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Flashback: The lawsuit comes one day after Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), a potential running mate for JD Vance in 2028, accused Smith of perjury at Tuesday's hearing but got his facts wrong and was later corrected by Smith and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.). The mistake went viral and drew extensive criticism on social media. Catch up quick: In October 2025, the GOP-led House Judiciary Committee released highly redacted documents showing that the FBI had investigated approximately 160 Republican figures as part of its probe into Trump's false claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. The probe, known as Arctic Frost, sought to identify those who "conspired to corruptly obstruct the United States Congress' certification of the 2020 Presidential election results by submitting allegedly fraudulent elector certificates." By the numbers: The lawsuit claims the Arctic Frost probe subpoenaed records associated with at least 20 Republican members of Congress. The lawsuit claims about 400 Republican individuals and organizations were targeted. The lawsuit says records involving roughly 4,782 Trump donors, including 102 Tennesseans, contained home addresses, bank account numbers and signatures. The bottom line: Blackburn's lawsuit extends the legal and political fight over the Justice Department's investigations into Trump after he left office. Trump and his allies have vowed to continue probing those who investigated or crossed the president, including New York Attorney General Letitia James (D), former FBI chief James Comey and Sen.
